turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in, Mrs. Keller. I'll grab the vitals before Dr. Shah steps in. Shoes off for the scale if you can manage it.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh sure, yes, I can manage, I just go slow with the cane. My daughter Linda drove me, and the parking lot was a complete maze, we circled twice. But I'm fine, really, I am.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Mom, just step up. I'll hold the cane.

[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Weight a hundred and fifty-two pounds. Last time in March you were sixty-eight, that was kilos on the old chart. Blood pressure is one oh nine over seventy-seven, and your last pressure was one-forty. Heart rate eighty-eight, no, eighty-four a minute, temp thirty-eight point three celsius.

[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty-eight point three, is that high? I felt a little warm in the car, but the heater was blasting and Linda had her coat on. I thought it was just the car, you know how those heaters stick on high.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mrs. Keller. Six-week hip check, right?

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the right hip, replaced six weeks ago. Well I was going to say eight because the pre-op visits dragged on, no, the surgery itself was six weeks ago Tuesday, at St. Mary's. Dr. Alvarez did it, and everyone there was lovely.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh the hip aches, not sharp like the first week, more a deep ache when I walk to the mailbox, that's maybe forty steps, and at night if I lie on that side. It's better than it was, I can tell. The first ten days I couldn't get comfortable in that old recliner at all.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Scale of one to ten. Now.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): A three. Maybe a four if I've been up awhile. Mostly three, sitting here it's a three.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She was worn out after the grocery store yesterday. That lot is uphill.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I was tired, yes, the lot is uphill, that's all, Linda. Not a big setback, I just needed the couch for a bit.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Swelling in the calf?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I look every night, both calves, no swelling, no redness, my neighbor had a clot and she told me to check. So I check, with the lamp on, and there's nothing there.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath? Chest pain?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain at all. I get winded on the stairs but that's been years, not new, I just pause on the landing. I don't get that tight feeling or anything scary.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The stairs thing is old, Doctor. Since her knees, honestly.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me see the wound.

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I kept the dressing on till the home nurse said stop, that was week two. I've been washing it with plain soap, not the perfumed one, the white bar, and patting it dry. Someone at church said vitamin E oil but I didn't put any on, I wasn't sure.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Incision is closed. No drainage. No redness. Healed.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh good. I thought that little scab at the bottom might be something, but it's tiny, like a dot.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Using a cane?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the wooden one, it's really just a stick my husband had. A walker is steadier but the cane fits in the car, and Linda's trunk is full of the kids' soccer stuff. They taught me the cane goes in the left hand, umm, because the new hip is the right one.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Aspirin?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, for the clots, the blood thinner one. I take aspirin three hundred and twenty-five, no, that's what my sister takes for her heart, I'm on the eighty-one milligram, once a day. Morning, with breakfast, I don't skip it.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Painkiller?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Tylenol, extra strength, five hundred milligrams, two tablets, three times a day. I was on oxicodone, five milligrams, but I stopped that, umm, about two weeks ago. It made me foggy and I didn't like how the morning felt.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She still has the bottle in the cabinet. I don't think she's touched it since.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't. I don't want it. It's just sitting there behind the band-aids.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Allergies?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I'm aware of. Penicillin was fine when I had that tooth, years back, no rash or anything.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fever at home? Chills?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't take my temperature, we don't have a thermometer in the house. I felt warm in the car, like I said, but no chills, no shaking. I slept with the one blanket, same as always.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She wouldn't let me buy a thermometer. I offered, twice.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): Appetite?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. I eat, maybe smaller portions, oatmeal, soup, and Linda brings those casseroles on Sundays. I'm not skipping meals.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Temp's up a little. Wound looks clean. I'm not calling this an infection.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. Should I worry, though? My cousin had an infection after her knee and she was in the hospital nine days, and the whole family...
[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. Not from what I see. Walk as you are, cane is fine. Keep the aspirin, eighty-one, daily, and the Tylenol as you are, don't go over three thousand milligrams a day.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Two tablets three times is three thousand, yes, I counted it on a napkin once. Six times five hundred. I won't add any extra, even if the ache bumps up.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the calf swells, or you get chest pain, go to the ER. We might do a scan if the ache does not settle.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Like an ultrasound?
[SEG0044] person_4 (DOCTOR): If we need it. Not today. Come back in two weeks. Front desk will book it.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, alright. Should I keep checking the calves every night? I set a phone alarm for eight, both legs, and I write it in the little notebook by the phone.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Once a day is enough. Call if it changes. That's it.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thank you. Mom, cane. Watch the rug.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. And thanks for not rushing me on the scale, my balance is still a whole project. We'll be out front if the desk wants the insurance card, it's the blue one, not the expired one.

spec.situation: Older patient six weeks after a hip replacement with a daughter; wound healed; walks with a stick; takes aspirin for clots and painkiller; swelling of the calf asked about and denied.

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

Negative finding asked and answered: no fever documented at home because she did not measure her temperature / has no thermometer at home.
Medication discontinuation timing missing: oxycodone 5 mg was stopped about two weeks ago.
Past surgical history detail missing: right hip replacement was done at St. Mary's by Dr. Alvarez.
Mobility/history detail missing: patient uses a cane and goes slow with it; balance is still impaired enough that getting on the scale is difficult.
